questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle with an acute angle θ, sin θ is equal to:
questions.explanation: SOH: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse. Adjacent ÷ hypotenuse is cos θ, and opposite ÷ adjacent is tan θ.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, the hypotenuse is:
options: the side next to the angle θ
the shortest side of the triangle
the side opposite the right angle
the side opposite the angle θ
questions.explanation: The hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle and is the longest side. The sides named opposite and adjacent depend on which acute angle is being used.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, the ratio adjacent ÷ hypotenuse for an angle θ is:
questions.explanation: CAH: cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse. Sine uses the opposite side over the hypotenuse, and tangent uses opposite over adjacent.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 12 cm and an angle of 35°. The side opposite the 35° angle, correct to two decimal places, is:
questions.explanation: sin 35° = x/12, so x = 12 sin 35° = 6.88 cm. Using cosine gives 9.83 cm, which is the side adjacent to the angle.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, the side adjacent to a 40° angle is 8 m. The side opposite the 40° angle, correct to two decimal places, is:
questions.explanation: tan 40° = x/8, so x = 8 tan 40° = 6.71 m. Dividing instead, 8 ÷ tan 40° = 9.53 m, swaps the opposite and adjacent sides.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, the side opposite a 28° angle is 5 cm. The hypotenuse, correct to two decimal places, is:
questions.explanation: sin 28° = 5/h, so h = 5 ÷ sin 28° = 10.65 cm. Multiplying, 5 × sin 28° = 2.35 cm, gives a value shorter than the opposite side, which a hypotenuse can never be.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, the side adjacent to a 52° angle is 15 m. The hypotenuse, correct to two decimal places, is:
questions.explanation: cos 52° = 15/h, so h = 15 ÷ cos 52° = 24.36 m. Dividing by sin 52° gives 19.04 m, which treats the 15 m side as opposite the angle.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, the side opposite angle θ is 7 cm and the hypotenuse is 10 cm. Correct to one decimal place, θ is:
questions.explanation: sin θ = 7/10, so θ = sin⁻¹(0.7) = 44.4°. Using cos⁻¹(0.7) = 45.6° finds the other acute angle, and tan⁻¹(0.7) = 35.0° uses the wrong ratio.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, the side opposite angle θ is 9 m and the side adjacent to it is 4 m. Correct to one decimal place, θ is:
questions.explanation: tan θ = 9/4, so θ = tan⁻¹(2.25) = 66.0°. Inverting the ratio, tan⁻¹(4/9) = 24.0°, gives the other acute angle.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, the side adjacent to angle θ is 6 cm and the hypotenuse is 11 cm. Correct to one decimal place, θ is:
questions.explanation: cos θ = 6/11, so θ = cos⁻¹(6/11) = 56.9°. Using sin⁻¹(6/11) = 33.1° treats the 6 cm side as opposite θ.

questions.stem: A 5 m ladder leans against a vertical wall and makes an angle of 72° with the level ground. How far up the wall does it reach, correct to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: The ladder is the hypotenuse and the wall height is opposite the 72° angle: 5 sin 72° = 4.76 m. Using cosine gives 1.55 m, the distance of the foot from the wall.

questions.stem: A wheelchair ramp rises 0.8 m over a horizontal distance of 9.6 m. The angle the ramp makes with the horizontal, correct to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: tan θ = rise/run = 0.8/9.6, so θ = tan⁻¹(0.0833) = 4.8°. The value 85.2° comes from inverting the ratio, which gives the angle with the vertical.

questions.stem: A room is 5 m long, 4 m wide and 3 m high. A string runs from one floor corner to the opposite ceiling corner. The angle the string makes with the floor, correct to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: The floor diagonal is √(5² + 4²) = √41 = 6.40 m. The string, the floor diagonal and the 3 m vertical edge form a right-angled triangle, so θ = tan⁻¹(3/6.40) = 25.1°. Using the 5 m length instead of the floor diagonal gives 31.0°.

questions.stem: A cyclist rides 300 m due east, then 400 m due south. How far is she from her starting point in a straight line?
questions.explanation: The two legs are at right angles, so the distance is √(300² + 400²) = √250 000 = 500 m. Adding the legs gives 700 m, the distance travelled, not the straight-line distance.

questions.stem: For a triangle with two sides a and b and the angle C between them, the area is:
questions.explanation: The perpendicular height from the end of side a is a sin C, so the area is 1/2 × b × a sin C = 1/2 ab sin C. Leaving out the 1/2 doubles the area.

questions.stem: A triangular garden bed has a base of 14 m and a perpendicular height of 9 m. Its area is:
questions.explanation: Area = 1/2 × base × height = 1/2 × 14 × 9 = 63 m². Forgetting the 1/2 gives 126 m², the area of a rectangle with the same base and height.

questions.stem: A triangle has sides of 8 cm and 11 cm with an included angle of 50°. Its area, correct to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: Area = 1/2 × 8 × 11 × sin 50° = 44 × 0.766 = 33.7 cm². Using cos 50° gives 28.3 cm², and 44 cm² leaves out the sine altogether.

questions.stem: An equilateral triangle has sides of 6 cm. Using Area = 1/2 ab sin C, its exact area is:
questions.explanation: Each angle is 60°, so the area is 1/2 × 6 × 6 × sin 60° = 18 × √3/2 = 9√3 cm², about 15.6 cm². The value 18√3 cm² leaves out the 1/2.

questions.stem: A triangular block of land has two sides of 40 m and 55 m with an included angle of 110°. Its area, correct to the nearest square metre, is:
questions.explanation: Area = 1/2 × 40 × 55 × sin 110° = 1100 × 0.9397 = 1034 m². The rule works for an obtuse included angle; 376 m² comes from using cos 110° and dropping its negative sign.

questions.stem: A triangle has sides of 8 cm and 10 cm and an area of 30 cm². The included angle is acute. Correct to one decimal place, the included angle is:
questions.explanation: 30 = 1/2 × 8 × 10 × sin C gives sin C = 30/40 = 0.75, so C = sin⁻¹(0.75) = 48.6°. Forgetting the 1/2 gives sin C = 0.375 and 22.0°.

questions.stem: When an observer looks up at an object, the angle of elevation is measured:
options: down from the vertical to the line of sight
up from the horizontal to the line of sight
down from the horizontal to the line of sight
up from the vertical to the line of sight
questions.explanation: An angle of elevation is the angle between the horizontal and a line of sight looking up at an object. Looking down from the horizontal gives an angle of depression.

questions.stem: From the top of a tower, the angle of depression of a car is 24°. The angle of elevation of the top of the tower from the car is:
questions.explanation: The two horizontal lines are parallel, so the angle of depression and the angle of elevation are alternate angles and are equal. The value 66° is the angle with the vertical.

questions.stem: From a point 50 m from the base of a tree on level ground, the angle of elevation of the top of the tree is 32°. The height of the tree, correct to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: tan 32° = h/50, so h = 50 tan 32° = 31.2 m. Dividing, 50 ÷ tan 32° = 80.0 m, swaps the opposite and adjacent sides.

questions.stem: From the top of a 60 m cliff, the angle of depression of a boat is 18°. How far is the boat from the base of the cliff, correct to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: The angle of elevation from the boat is also 18°, so tan 18° = 60/d and d = 60 ÷ tan 18° = 184.7 m. The value 194.2 m is the line-of-sight distance, 60 ÷ sin 18°.

questions.stem: A kite flies on a taut 40 m string that makes an angle of elevation of 55° with the ground, measured from where the string is held. How high is the kite above that point, correct to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: The string is the hypotenuse, so the height is 40 sin 55° = 32.8 m. Using cosine gives 22.9 m, which is the horizontal distance.

questions.stem: A drone hovers 120 m above level ground. The angle of depression from the drone to a parked car is 25°. The horizontal distance from the drone to the car, correct to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: tan 25° = 120/d, so d = 120 ÷ tan 25° = 257.3 m. The value 283.9 m is the direct line of sight, 120 ÷ sin 25°.

questions.stem: Sam's eyes are 1.6 m above level ground. Standing 25 m from a flagpole, he measures the angle of elevation of the top as 28°. The height of the flagpole, correct to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: The triangle gives the height above eye level: 25 tan 28° = 13.3 m. Adding Sam's eye height gives 13.3 + 1.6 = 14.9 m; 13.3 m forgets the eye height.

questions.stem: From point A the angle of elevation of the top of a building is 30°. From point B, 20 m closer on the same level line, it is 45°. The height of the building, correct to two decimal places, is:
questions.explanation: Let the distance from B be d. Then h = d (tan 45°) and h = (d + 20) tan 30°, so d = (d + 20)/√3, giving d = 20/(√3 − 1) = 27.32 m. Since tan 45° = 1, h = d = 27.32 m.

questions.stem: From the top of a lighthouse 45 m above sea level, the angles of depression of two boats directly in line on the same side are 20° and 12°. The distance between the boats, correct to one decimal place, is:
questions.explanation: The nearer boat is 45 ÷ tan 20° = 123.6 m from the base and the farther one 45 ÷ tan 12° = 211.7 m. The distance between them is 211.7 − 123.6 = 88.1 m.

questions.stem: A true bearing is measured:
options: clockwise from east, as three digits
from north or south towards east or west
clockwise from north, as three digits
anticlockwise from north, as three digits
questions.explanation: True bearings start at north and go clockwise, written with three digits such as 045°T. Measuring from north or south towards east or west describes compass bearings such as N45°E.

questions.stem: The true bearing 135°T, written as a compass bearing, is:
questions.explanation: 135° clockwise from north lies between east (090°) and south (180°), 45° from south towards east, so it is S45°E.

questions.stem: The compass bearing N30°W, written as a true bearing, is:
questions.explanation: N30°W is 30° west of north, which is 360° − 30° = 330° measured clockwise from north. The value 300°T is 30° north of west, which is N60°W.

questions.stem: Town B is on a bearing of 070°T from town A. The bearing of town A from town B is:
questions.explanation: The back bearing differs by 180°: 070° + 180° = 250°T. The value 290°T comes from subtracting 70° from 360°, which is a reflection, not the reverse direction.

questions.stem: A ship sails 20 km on a bearing of 060°T. How far east of its starting point is it, correct to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: The bearing makes 60° with north, so the eastward distance is opposite that angle: 20 sin 60° = 17.32 km. The value 10.00 km is 20 cos 60°, the distance north.

questions.stem: A yacht sails 15 km on a bearing of 140°T. How far south of its starting point is it, correct to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: The bearing 140°T is 40° east of south, so the southward distance is adjacent to the 40° angle: 15 cos 40° = 11.49 km. The value 9.64 km is 15 sin 40°, the distance east.

questions.stem: A plane flies 200 km on a bearing of 300°T. How far west of its starting point is it, correct to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: The bearing 300°T is 60° west of north, so the westward distance is 200 sin 60° = 173.2 km. The value 100.0 km is 200 cos 60°, the distance north.

questions.stem: A hiker walks 6 km due north and then 8 km due east. Her distance and true bearing from the starting point are:
questions.explanation: The distance is √(6² + 8²) = 10 km. The angle east of north is tan⁻¹(8/6) = 53.1°, so the bearing is 053°T. Using tan⁻¹(6/8) gives 037°T, the angle measured from east.

questions.stem: A boat travels 9 km due south and then 12 km due west. The true bearing of the boat from its starting point, to the nearest degree, is:
questions.explanation: The boat is south-west of the start, at tan⁻¹(12/9) = 53.1° west of south. Measured clockwise from north this is 180° + 53° = 233°T. Using tan⁻¹(9/12) gives 217°T.
